newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey says Iraqi oil pipeline technically ready.
newsitem.headline: Turkey says Iraqi oil pipeline technically ready.

text.p: A twin oil pipeline from Iraq to Turkey is technically ready for use under a U.N. plan that will allow Baghdad to sell oil to buy food for its people, Turkish officials said on Tuesday.
"We had already made it ready months ago when talk of its reopening was on the agenda in the summer," said a senior oil official, who declined to be named.
He said Turkey's private construction company Tekfen, which originally built the pipeline, had repaired parts damaged during the Gulf War in 1991.
"Apart from work by U.N. monitors to make sure the pipeline and its control units function properly, there is nothing to be done. Turkey has completed its job," the official told Reuters.

Iraq said on Monday it had agreed to all U.N. conditions for the delayed "oil-for-food" deal, under which it can sell oil worth $2 billion over six months on a renewable basis to buy food and medicine. Its people have suffering under a U.N. embargo since Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990.
The plan was delayed by differences over how to carry it out, including Iraqi insistence on controlling the number, makeup and movement of U.N. observers who would monitor implementation.
The United Nations also postponed deploying observers after Baghdad sent troops into Kurdish-held northern Iraq in late August to support one side in a Kurdish conflict.

U.N. officials said the United Nations would have to send experts back to northern Iraq to ensure that oil metering equipment on the Iraq-Turkish border, which had not been in working order, was functioning.

The bulk of Iraqi oil exports are to flow through the 986-km (613-mile) pipeline from Iraq's Kirkuk oilfields to Turkey's southern Ceyhan port, with the rest exported via the Gulf port of Mina al-Bakr.
Iraq's U.N. ambassador, Nizar Hamdoon, said the pipeline to Turkey "will definitely be ready by the first week of December."
Turkey's state-controlled Anatolian news agency, quoting unnamed U.N. officials in New York, said oil could begin flowing through the pipeline from December 5.

The Dutch firm Saybolt will inspect the pipeline to ensure faulty equipment at Iraq's Zakho station near the Turkish border is operational. Lloyds of London this week will inspect facilities for imports.
Turkey's state oil refiner Tupras had asked for 2.1 million tonnes of Iraq's oil sales in the first six months of the plan.

Turkey earlier said transit fees for using the pipeline, shut since Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, depended on oil prices. It had a tariff of 72 cents per barrel for up to 750,000 barrels per day before the shutdown.
